paragraphs.heading: What it is
paragraphs.text: Schrödinger's cat is a thought experiment about quantum superposition, where a system is described as a combination of several possibilities. Picture a cat sealed in a box with a flask of poison and a radioactive source. If a detector such as a Geiger counter picks up a single atom decaying, the flask breaks, the poison escapes and the cat dies. If no atom decays, the cat lives.

paragraphs.heading: Alive, dead, or both
paragraphs.text: Because the cat's fate hangs on a random subatomic event, it can be thought of as alive and dead together while nobody looks, which is why the setup is called a paradox. Yet anyone who opens the box sees a cat that is either alive or dead, never both. Our intuition says a cat cannot be in two states at once, while the quantum description demands exactly that. So the experiment asks how long a superposition can survive, and at what point, if ever, it collapses into one result.

paragraphs.heading: How it began
paragraphs.text: Erwin Schrödinger came up with it in 1935, during a discussion with Albert Einstein. It answered the EPR article by Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen, which argued that quantum mechanics was incomplete because a two-particle system does not split apart even when the particles end up far from each other. In their letters, Einstein pointed out that an unstable keg of gunpowder would, after some time, be in a superposition of exploded and unexploded. Schrödinger went further, showing how a large system could in principle be put into superposition by tying it to a quantum particle that was in one.

paragraphs.heading: Meant as a criticism
paragraphs.text: Schrödinger did not want anyone to take dead-and-alive cats seriously. He meant the example as a reductio ad absurdum, using an absurd picture to show up the flaws he saw in the existing view of quantum mechanics. In his account, the position of Bohr and Heisenberg would keep the cat both alive and dead until the state was observed. The experiment was never meant to be done on a real cat; it was a simple picture of how atoms behave.

paragraphs.heading: Why it lasted
paragraphs.text: Though it started as a critique, the cat ended up among the founding ideas of quantum mechanics. In modern terms it captures the measurement problem: theory describes the cat as a mix of two outcomes, yet only one is ever seen. Physicists use it to compare interpretations of quantum mechanics, some of which treat the alive-and-dead superposition as real while others do not. It has also kept a lasting place in popular culture.

paragraphs.heading: Could it be done for real
paragraphs.text: Experiments at the scale of atoms have shown that very small objects can exist in superpositions. Doing the same with something as large as a cat, though, would raise serious technical problems. Schrödinger had argued that, in principle, tying a large system to a quantum particle in superposition would pass that superposition on.
